title: Architecture aware compilation of quantum circuits via lazy synthesis
abstract: <jats:p>Qubit routing is a key problem for quantum circuit compilation. It consists in rewriting a quantum circuit by adding the least possible number of instructions to make the circuit compliant with some architecture&apos;s connectivity constraints. Usually, this problem is tackled via either SWAP insertion techniques or re-synthesis of portions of the circuit using architecture aware synthesis algorithms. In this work, we propose a meta-heuristic that couples the iterative approach of SWAP insertion techniques with greedy architecture-aware synthesis routines. We propose two new compilation algorithms based on this meta-heuristic and compare their performances to state-of-the-art quantum circuit compilation techniques for several standard classes of quantum circuits and show significant reduction in the entangling gate overhead due to compilation.</jats:p>

title: Quantum circuit compilation and hybrid computation using Pauli-based computation
abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Pauli-based computation (PBC) is driven by a sequence of adaptively chosen, non-destructive measurements of Pauli observables. Any quantum circuit written in terms of the Clifford+
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>T</mml:mi>
                    </mml:math>
                    gate set and having
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>
                    </mml:math>
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>T</mml:mi>
                    </mml:math>
                    gates can be compiled into a PBC on
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>
                    </mml:math>
                    qubits. Here we propose practical ways of implementing PBC as adaptive quantum circuits and provide code to do the required classical side-processing. Our schemes reduce the number of quantum gates to
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>O</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo>
                      <mml:msup>
                        <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>
                        <mml:mn>2</mml:mn>
                      </mml:msup>
                      <mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo>
                    </mml:math>
                    (from a previous
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>O</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo>
                      <mml:msup>
                        <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>
                        <mml:mn>3</mml:mn>
                      </mml:msup>
                      <mml:mrow class="MJX-TeXAtom-ORD">
                        <mml:mo>/</mml:mo>
                      </mml:mrow>
                      <mml:mi>log</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mo>&#x2061;</mml:mo>
                      <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo>
                    </mml:math>
                    scaling) and space/time trade-offs are discussed which lead to a reduction of the depth from
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>O</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo>
                      <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mi>log</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mo>&#x2061;</mml:mo>
                      <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo>
                    </mml:math>
                    to
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>O</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mo stretchy="false">(</mml:mo>
                      <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>
                      <mml:mo stretchy="false">)</mml:mo>
                    </mml:math>
                    within our schemes, at the cost of
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>t</mml:mi>
                    </mml:math>
                    additional auxiliary qubits. We compile examples of random and hidden-shift quantum circuits into adaptive PBC circuits. We also simulate hybrid quantum computation, where a classical computer effectively extends the working memory of a small quantum computer by
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>k</mml:mi>
                    </mml:math>
                    virtual qubits, at a cost exponential in
                    <mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML">
                      <mml:mi>k</mml:mi>
                    </mml:math>
                    . Our results demonstrate the practical advantage of PBC techniques for circuit compilation and hybrid computation.
                  </jats:p>
